specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: This paper proposes a neural encoder-decoder transition-based parser for semantic graph parsing (MRS/DMRS/EDS/AMR), claiming to be the 'first full-coverage neural MRS parser.' The core contribution combines arc-eager transition systems with hard attention pointer networks and stack-based features for joint node/alignment prediction. Evidence-based analysis reveals a pattern of claims that are partially supported, overstated, or contradicted by the paper's own results. The 'first' claim is defensible but narrowly scoped (depends on 'full-coverage' and 'neural' definitions; prior work achieved MRS parsing with grammar access). Hard attention superiority is demonstrated on DMRS (84.65% vs 81.53% EDM) but contradicted on AMR (59.83% vs 59.88% Smatch), suggesting representation-specific rather than general superiority. Stack-based improvements are modest (0.63 EDM) and lack statistical significance testing. The speedup claim (70x) conflates GPU hardware with batching; unbatched speedup is only 5.6x. The MRS vs AMR parseability claim (86.69% vs 83% upper bound) conflates representation difficulty with training data quality differences (DeepBank inter-annotator agreement 0.94 vs AMR 0.71). AMR results (60.11% Smatch) are substantially weaker than MRS (86.50% Smatch), suggesting the architecture may be MRS-specific. Oracle errors (1-2% EDM) and tokenization mismatches limit achievable accuracy. Greedy decoding may miss better parses; no beam search comparison provided. Test set is biased toward sentences parsable by ERG; 15% coverage gap means evaluation is incomplete. Overall, the paper makes solid incremental contributions to semantic parsing but overstates novelty and generalizability claims while undersupporting key assertions with rigorous evidence.
logical_argument_graph: Premise 1: Neural encoder-decoder models have achieved state-of-the-art on dependency and constituency parsing (Kiperwasser & Goldberg 2016, Dyer et al. 2015).
Premise 2: Deep learning enables global conditioning for predicting complex structures without increasing algorithmic complexity.
Premise 3: Transition-based parsing is efficient and well-understood for dependency parsing.
Conclusion 1: Combining transition-based parsing with neural sequence modeling should enable robust parsing of linguistically deep semantic graphs.
Premise 4: Arc-eager transition systems have been adapted for graph parsing (Titov et al. 2009, Gómez-Rodríguez & Nivre 2010).
Premise 5: Hard attention with pointer networks can predict token alignments from supervised data.
Conclusion 2: Arc-eager transition system + hard attention + stack-based features should outperform soft attention baselines.
Evidence for Conclusion 2: DMRS results show 84.65% EDM (hard) vs 81.53% EDM (soft) on development set.
Counterevidence for Conclusion 2: AMR results show 59.83% Smatch (hard) vs 59.88% Smatch (soft), contradicting the claim.
Premise 6: Stack-based features capture transition system state information.
Conclusion 3: Stack-based features should improve over pure attention models.
Evidence for Conclusion 3: DMRS shows 85.28% EDM (stack) vs 84.65% EDM (hard attention) on development set.
Uncertainty: Improvement is modest (0.63 EDM) and statistical significance not tested.
Premise 7: GPU batch processing enables order-of-magnitude speedup over CPU-based grammar parsers.
Conclusion 4: Neural parser is 70x faster than ACE parser.
Counterevidence for Conclusion 4: Speedup conflates GPU hardware (529.42 tokens/sec batched) with unbatched version (41.63 tokens/sec, only 5.6x faster than ACE 7.47 tokens/sec).
Premise 8: MRS has higher inter-annotator agreement (0.94) than AMR (0.71).
Premise 9: MRS parser achieves 86.69% Smatch; AMR upper bound is ~83% F1.
Conclusion 5: MRS is a more parseable semantic representation than AMR.
Counterevidence for Conclusion 5: Comparison conflates representation difficulty with training data quality; no controlled experiment isolating representation difficulty from annotation quality.
Premise 10: Unlexicalized predicate prediction reduces vocabulary size and improves generalization.
Conclusion 6: Unlexicalized models should outperform lexicalized models.
Evidence for Conclusion 6: DMRS shows 82.56% EDM (unlexicalized) vs 81.35% EDM (lexicalized) on development set.
Uncertainty: Improvement is modest (1.21 EDM) and statistical significance not tested.

identified_claims.claim_label: First full-coverage neural MRS parser
identified_claims.claim_text: This is the first full-coverage semantic graph parser for Minimal Recursion Semantics (MRS) using neural encoder-decoder transition-based architecture without access to underlying grammars.
evidence: Abstract: 'We propose a neural encoder-decoder transition-based parser which is the first full-coverage semantic graph parser for Minimal Recursion Semantics (MRS).'

Introduction: 'The only previous approach to parsing and disambiguating full MRS structures (as opposed to bilexical semantic graphs derived from, but simplifying MRS) were based on the ERG (Toutanova et al., 2005); this approach has high precision but incomplete coverage.'

Introduction: 'Our main contribution is to develop a fast and robust parser for full MRS-based semantic graphs. We exploit the power of global conditioning enabled by deep learning to predict linguistically deep graphs incrementally. The model does not have access to the underlying ERG or syntactic structures from which the MRS analyses were originally derived.'

No explicit comparison to concurrent neural approaches to MRS parsing is provided; concurrent work may exist.
Coverage is only demonstrated on DeepBank test set (sentences with ERG parses); generalization to out-of-domain text unclear.
15% of original corpus lacks ERG parses; evaluation is incomplete on full corpus.

Results text: 'The results show that the arc-eager models performs better than those based on top-down representation. For the arc-eager model we use hard attention, due to the natural interpretation of the alignment prediction corresponding to the transition system.'
uncertainty_flags: Comparison is limited to DMRS development set; no soft attention results reported for arc-eager model on test set.
Hard attention requires supervised alignments (from MRS annotations), which may not be available for all semantic representations.
Difference between hard and soft attention on top-down is modest (1.22 EDM); statistical significance not reported.
AMR results (Table 5) show soft attention performs comparably or better (59.88% vs 59.83% Smatch), directly contradicting the general claim.
Claim is stated as general principle but evidence is representation-specific (DMRS); generalization to AMR is not supported.

identified_claims.claim_label: Stack-based features improve over pure attention
identified_claims.claim_text: Stack-based embedding features improve parsing accuracy from 79.68% to 84.16% F1 on DMRS compared to attention-based baselines.
evidence: Abstract: 'Our parser is more accurate than attention-based baselines on MRS, and on an additional Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) benchmark.'
Table 2: TD soft 81.53 EDM → AE stack 85.28 EDM (development set).
Text: 'The arc-eager stack-based architecture improves further over the model that purely relies on the hard attention.'
uncertainty_flags: The 84.16% figure in abstract appears to refer to test set (Table 3: 85.48 EDM), not development set; citation is unclear.
Baseline comparison is unclear: 79.68% is not explicitly identified in tables; may refer to soft attention baseline or some other model.
Improvement from hard to stack on arc-eager is only 0.63 EDM (84.65% to 85.28%); statistical significance not tested.
Stack features require access to transition system state; generalizability to other architectures unclear.
Comparison conflates multiple architectural changes (hard attention, stack features, linearization); ablation is incomplete.

identified_claims.claim_label: Order of magnitude speedup over grammar-based parser
identified_claims.claim_text: GPU batch processing makes the neural parser an order of magnitude faster than the high-precision grammar-based ACE parser.
evidence: Abstract: 'GPU batch processing makes it an order of magnitude faster than a high-precision grammar-based parser.'

Section 5.4: 'The batched (stack-based) implementation parses 529.42 tokens per second, using a batch size of 128. In comparison, the setting of ACE for which we reported accuracies parses 7.47 tokens per second.'
Speedup calculation: 529.42 / 7.47 ≈ 70.8x (approximately order of magnitude).
uncertainty_flags: Speedup is specific to batched implementation with batch size 128; unbatched version is only 41.63 tokens/sec (5.6x faster than ACE 7.47 tokens/sec).
ACE speed varies with configuration: 11.07 tokens/sec at 87.7% coverage, 15.11 tokens/sec at 77.8% coverage; comparison uses slowest ACE configuration.
Comparison is not apples-to-apples: ACE achieves 89.58% EDM vs neural parser 85.48% EDM; speedup comes at accuracy cost.
Batch processing advantage may not apply to online/streaming scenarios or single-sentence parsing.
Hardware differences (GPU vs CPU) confound the comparison; speedup is not purely algorithmic.
Claim of 'order of magnitude' is technically correct (70x ≈ 10^1.85) but misleading without acknowledging batching requirement and accuracy trade-off.

identified_claims.claim_label: MRS more parseable than AMR
identified_claims.claim_text: MRS (86.69% Smatch) is a more parseable semantic representation than AMR, which has an upper bound of ~83% F1 due to inter-annotator agreement.
evidence: Abstract: 'Further, the 86.69% Smatch score of our MRS parser is higher than the upper-bound on AMR parsing, making MRS an attractive choice as a semantic representation.'

Introduction: 'the size of the available training data is still relatively small, and inter-annotator agreement has been shown to be relatively low, placing on upper bound of 83% F1 on the expected parser performance.'
Table 3: DMRS test set Smatch 86.50; Table 6: AMR test set Smatch 60.11.
uncertainty_flags: Comparison conflates representation difficulty with parser quality: MRS parser benefits from grammar-derived training data (DeepBank) with high inter-annotator agreement (0.94).
AMR upper bound (83%) is cited without source; actual inter-annotator agreement on LDC2015E86 not provided in paper.
Smatch metric differs between DMRS (EDM-based) and AMR (Smatch); direct comparison may not be valid.
AMR results (60.11% Smatch) are substantially lower than MRS (86.50% Smatch), but this may reflect parser quality rather than representation difficulty.
No controlled experiment isolating representation difficulty from training data quality, annotation agreement, or parser architecture.
Claim assumes inter-annotator agreement directly determines parser upper bound, but this relationship is not established.

identified_claims.claim_label: Arc-eager outperforms top-down for MRS
identified_claims.claim_text: Arc-eager linearization outperforms top-down linearization for MRS; in-order outperforms monotone for AMR.
evidence: Table 1: TD unlex 81.72 EDM vs AE delex 82.56 EDM (development).
Table 2: TD soft 81.53 EDM vs AE hard 84.65 EDM (development).

Section 5.4: 'The arc-eager unlexicalized linearization gives the best performance, down linearization, even though the model has to learn to model the transition stack inside the recurrent states without any supervision of the semantics of transition actions.'
Section 5.5: 'In contrast to DMRS parsing, the in-order linearization gives better results than the monotone one. We hypothesize that this is due to the non-compositional nature of AMR.'
uncertainty_flags: Improvement of arc-eager over top-down on DMRS is modest (0.84 EDM on development).
For AMR, arc-eager does not outperform top-down (Table 5: AE hard delex 59.83 vs TD soft delex 59.88 Smatch); claim is partially contradicted.
Hypothesis about non-compositionality is speculative; no direct evidence provided.
Linearization choice may interact with other architectural choices (hard vs soft attention, stack features); ablation is incomplete.
Statistical significance of differences not reported.
Claim conflates two separate findings (arc-eager for MRS, in-order for AMR) as if they follow from a single principle.

identified_claims.claim_label: Unlexicalized predicates generalize better
identified_claims.claim_text: Unlexicalized predicate prediction generalizes better than lexicalized prediction.
evidence: Table 1: TD lex 81.44 EDM vs TD unlex 81.72 EDM; AE lex 81.35 EDM vs AE delex 82.56 EDM.
Section 5.4: 'The unlexicalized models are more accurate, mostly due to their ability to generalize to sparse or unseen predicates occurring in the lexicon.'
Section 5.4: 'The unlexicalized models are also faster to train, as the decoder's output vocabulary is much smaller, reducing the expense of computing softmaxes over large vocabularies.'
uncertainty_flags: Improvements are modest (0.28-1.21 EDM).
Unlexicalized approach requires lemmatizer and dictionary lookup (Stanford CoreNLP), introducing external dependencies and potential error propagation.
For AMR, lexicalization is not explicitly tested; all reported models use unlexicalized concepts.
Generalization benefit may be specific to MRS/DMRS where lexical/non-lexical distinction is explicit.
No direct evaluation on out-of-vocabulary predicates or sparse phenomena; generalization claim is inferred from overall accuracy improvements.
Statistical significance not tested.

identified_claims.claim_label: Monotone ordering better for DMRS
identified_claims.claim_text: Monotone ordering (non-decreasing alignments) performs better than in-order ordering for arc-eager DMRS parsing.
evidence: Section 5.4: 'We compared the effect of different orderings of the predicates for the arc-eager model: The monotone ordering (with non-decreasing alignments) performs 0.44 EDM better that the in-order ordering, despite having to parse more non-planar dependencies.'
uncertainty_flags: Improvement is small (0.44 EDM).
Claim states monotone is better, but also notes it requires parsing more non-planar dependencies, which is computationally harder.
No test set results provided for this comparison; only development set mentioned.
Interaction with other architectural choices (hard attention, stack features) not explored.
Statistical significance not tested.

identified_claims.claim_label: Neural parser outperforms previous neural AMR parsers
identified_claims.claim_text: The arc-eager model outperforms previous sequence-to-sequence AMR parsers (Barzdins & Gosko 2016, Peng et al. 2017) and achieves 60.11% Smatch on test set.
evidence: Section 5.5: 'We show that even our neural baseline outperforms existing results for neural AMR parsing. The arc-eager model does not perform better than the top-down linearization, which we hypothesize is due to noise in the automatically-obtained alignments.'

Section 5.5: 'Our best neural model outperforms the baseline JAMR parser (Flanigan et al., 2014), but still lags behind the performance of state-of-the-art AMR parsers such as CAMR (Wang et al., 2016).'
Table 6: Arc-eager stack delex 60.11 Smatch (test set).
uncertainty_flags: Comparison to prior neural AMR parsers lacks explicit numbers; claims are qualitative.
Model lags behind state-of-the-art (CAMR), which uses external resources (syntax, SRL); comparison is not fair.
AMR results are substantially weaker than MRS results, limiting the strength of this claim.
Automatically-obtained alignments for AMR introduce noise; this is acknowledged but not quantified.
No ablation study isolating the contribution of arc-eager vs other architectural choices for AMR.
Claim that arc-eager 'does not perform better than top-down' contradicts earlier claim that arc-eager outperforms top-down.

identified_claims.claim_label: Model achieves full coverage on DeepBank
identified_claims.claim_text: The neural parser achieves full coverage on sentences in the DeepBank test set, unlike the grammar-based ACE parser.
evidence: Section 5.1: 'Parses are only provided for sentences for which the ERG has an analysis acceptable to the annotator – this means that we cannot evaluate parsing accuracy for sentences which the ERG cannot parse (approximately 15% of the original corpus).'

Section 5.4: 'Although the model is less accurate that a high-precision grammar-based parser on a test set of sentences parsable by that grammar, our model is an order of magnitude faster due to incremental prediction and a GPU batch processing implementation of the transition system.'
uncertainty_flags: Full coverage claim is implicit; not explicitly stated in results.
Coverage is only demonstrated on DeepBank test set (sentences with ERG parses); generalization to out-of-domain text unclear.
No evaluation on the 15% of sentences that ERG cannot parse; coverage claim is incomplete.
Greedy decoding may produce malformed parses; post-processing is used to enforce well-formedness, which may mask coverage issues.
No analysis of parse quality on difficult or rare phenomena.
Claim of 'full coverage' is not directly supported by evidence; only implicit in the fact that greedy decoding always produces some output.

strengths.title: Novel architectural synthesis for semantic graph parsing
strengths.description: The combination of arc-eager transition systems with hard attention pointer networks and stack-based features represents a coherent and well-motivated architectural design for semantic graph parsing. The paper clearly articulates why each component is necessary (e.g., hard attention for supervised alignments, stack features for transition system state).
evidence: Section 4.2-4.3: Clear motivation for hard attention ('natural interpretation of the alignment prediction corresponding to the transition system') and stack-based features.
Section 3.2: Detailed description of arc-eager transition system adapted for semantic graphs with joint node/alignment generation.
Tables 1-2: Systematic ablation showing contribution of each component (linearization, attention mechanism, stack features).

strengths.title: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple semantic representations
strengths.description: The paper evaluates the proposed architecture on three MRS-based representations (DMRS, EDS) and AMR, providing a more complete picture of generalizability than single-representation studies. Multiple metrics (EDM, EDM-Pred, EDM-Arg, Smatch, Concept F1) are reported.
evidence: Section 5.4: DMRS and EDS results with multiple metrics.
Section 5.5: AMR results with Smatch and Concept F1.
Tables 1-6: Systematic comparison across representations and model variants.

strengths.title: Practical engineering contribution: GPU batch processing for transition-based parsing
strengths.description: The implementation of stack-based transition-based parsing in static computation graphs with batch processing is a non-trivial engineering contribution that enables significant speedup (70x over unbatched CPU implementation). This is valuable for practical deployment.
evidence: Section 4.3: 'Our implementation of the stack-based model enables batch processing in static computation graphs, similar to Bowman et al. (2016). We maintain a stack of alignment indexes for each element in the batch, which is updated inside the computation graph after each parsing action.'
Section 5.4: Speed comparison showing 529.42 tokens/sec (batched) vs 41.63 tokens/sec (unbatched).

strengths.title: Clear presentation of transition system and linearization strategies
strengths.description: The paper provides clear explanations of the arc-eager transition system adapted for semantic graphs, including detailed examples (Figure 3) and comparison of linearization strategies (top-down vs arc-eager, in-order vs monotone). This makes the technical contribution accessible.
evidence: Section 3.1-3.2: Clear descriptions of linearization strategies with examples.
Figure 3: Detailed example of transition sequence with stack and buffer states.
Section 5.4: Systematic comparison of linearization choices with results.

strengths.title: Honest acknowledgment of limitations and error analysis
strengths.description: The paper acknowledges several limitations: oracle errors (1-2% EDM), tokenization mismatches, difficulty with end-span alignment prediction, and noise in automatically-obtained AMR alignments. This transparency is valuable for interpreting results.
evidence: Section 5.4: 'For the arc-eager representation, the oracle EDM is 99% for the lexicalized representation and 98.06% for the delexicalized representation. The remaining errors are due to discrepancies between the tokenization used by our system and the ERG tokenization.'
Section 5.4: 'EDM metrics excluding end-span prediction (-Start) show that our parser has relatively more difficulty in parsing end-span predictions than the grammar-based parser.'
Section 5.5: 'The arc-eager model does not perform better than the top-down linearization, which we hypothesize is due to noise in the automatically-obtained alignments.'

concerns.title: Lack of statistical significance testing for reported improvements
concerns.description: Key improvements are reported without statistical significance tests. For example, hard attention vs soft attention on DMRS shows 1.22 EDM improvement (81.53% to 82.75%), stack-based improvement is 0.63 EDM (84.65% to 85.28%), and unlexicalized vs lexicalized is 0.28-1.21 EDM. These modest improvements may not be statistically significant.
evidence: Table 1: TD soft 81.53 vs TD hard 82.75 (1.22 EDM difference, no significance test).
Table 2: AE hard 84.65 vs AE stack 85.28 (0.63 EDM difference, no significance test).
Section 5.4: No mention of significance testing for any reported improvements.
Prior stage digest (reviewer_1): 'several claims rest on modest empirical improvements (0.44–1.22 EDM), lack statistical significance testing.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct significance tests (e.g., bootstrap resampling, paired t-tests) for all reported improvements. Report confidence intervals or p-values. If improvements are not significant, revise claims accordingly.

concerns.title: Contradictory results between MRS and AMR undermine generalizability claims
concerns.description: Hard attention is claimed to outperform soft attention, but AMR results show soft attention performing comparably or better (59.88% vs 59.83% Smatch). Arc-eager is claimed to outperform top-down, but AMR results show top-down performing comparably or better (59.88% vs 59.83% Smatch). These contradictions suggest the architecture may be MRS-specific rather than general.
evidence: Table 2: DMRS shows AE hard 84.65 EDM (better than TD soft 81.53 EDM).
Table 5: AMR shows TD soft delex 59.88 Smatch vs AE hard delex 59.83 Smatch (soft attention slightly better).
Section 5.5: 'The arc-eager model does not perform better than the top-down linearization, which we hypothesize is due to noise in the automatically-obtained alignments.'
Prior stage digest (reviewer_2): 'Contradictory results between MRS and AMR undermine generalizability claims.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Investigate why hard attention and arc-eager work well for DMRS but not AMR. Provide deeper analysis of representation-specific factors (e.g., compositionality, alignment quality, predicate distribution). Revise claims to be representation-specific rather than general.

concerns.title: Speedup comparison conflates hardware, batching, and algorithmic improvements
concerns.description: The claim of 'order of magnitude speedup' (70x) conflates GPU hardware with batching. Unbatched speedup is only 5.6x (41.63 tokens/sec vs 7.47 tokens/sec). Batching is not always applicable (e.g., online/streaming scenarios). Comparison uses slowest ACE configuration (7.47 tokens/sec); faster configurations (11.07-15.11 tokens/sec) reduce speedup to 3.5-7x.
evidence: Section 5.4: 'The batched (stack-based) implementation parses 529.42 tokens per second, using a batch size of 128. In comparison, the setting of ACE for which we reported accuracies parses 7.47 tokens per second.'
Section 5.4: 'For the unbatched version of our model, the stack-based parser parses 41.63 tokens per second.'

Section 5.4: 'By restricting the memory usage of ACE, which restricts its coverage, we see that ACE can parse 11.07 tokens per second at 87.7% coverage, and 15.11 tokens per second at 77.8% coverage.'
Abstract: 'GPU batch processing makes it an order of magnitude faster than a high-precision grammar-based parser.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Separate hardware effects (GPU vs CPU) from algorithmic improvements (batching vs greedy decoding). Report unbatched speedup as primary metric. Acknowledge that batching requires buffering and is not applicable to all scenarios. Compare to ACE with comparable coverage/speed settings.

concerns.title: MRS vs AMR parseability claim conflates representation difficulty with training data quality
concerns.description: The claim that 'MRS is more parseable than AMR' (86.69% vs 83% upper bound) conflates representation difficulty with training data quality. DeepBank has inter-annotator agreement of 0.94, while AMR has 0.71. No controlled experiment isolates representation difficulty from annotation quality, training data size, or parser architecture.
evidence: Abstract: 'Further, the 86.69% Smatch score of our MRS parser is higher than the upper-bound on AMR parsing, making MRS an attractive choice as a semantic representation.'
Section 5.1: 'This approach has been shown to lead to high inter-annotator agreement: 0.94 against 0.71 for AMR (Bender et al., 2015).'
Introduction: 'inter-annotator agreement has been shown to be relatively low, placing on upper bound of 83% F1 on the expected parser performance.'
Prior stage digest (reviewer_4): 'MRS vs AMR parseability comparison conflates representation difficulty with training data quality.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Revise claim to acknowledge that MRS parser benefits from higher-quality training data (higher inter-annotator agreement, grammar-derived annotations). Conduct controlled experiment comparing parsers trained on data with similar annotation quality. Alternatively, frame as 'MRS is easier to parse with current methods given available training data' rather than 'MRS is inherently more parseable.'

concerns.title: Weak AMR results suggest architecture may be MRS-specific
concerns.description: AMR results (60.11% Smatch) are substantially weaker than MRS results (86.50% Smatch), and the paper acknowledges that arc-eager does not outperform top-down for AMR (contrary to MRS). This suggests the architecture may be optimized for MRS rather than being a general semantic graph parser.
evidence: Table 3: DMRS test set 86.50 Smatch.
Table 6: AMR test set 60.11 Smatch.
Section 5.5: 'The arc-eager model does not perform better than the top-down linearization, which we hypothesize is due to noise in the automatically-obtained alignments.'
Section 5.5: 'However, concept prediction remains a weakness of the model; Damonte et al. (2016) reports that state-of-the-art AMR parsers score between 79% and 83% on concept prediction.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Investigate why the architecture works well for MRS but poorly for AMR. Analyze differences in representation structure, alignment quality, and predicate distribution. Consider representation-specific modifications or acknowledge that the architecture is primarily designed for MRS-like representations.

concerns.title: Incomplete evaluation: 15% coverage gap and no out-of-domain testing
concerns.description: The test set is biased toward sentences parsable by ERG (85% of original corpus). No evaluation on the 15% of sentences that ERG cannot parse. No evaluation on out-of-domain text. Coverage claim is implicit rather than explicitly demonstrated.
evidence: Section 5.1: 'Parses are only provided for sentences for which the ERG has an analysis acceptable to the annotator – this means that we cannot evaluate parsing accuracy for sentences which the ERG cannot parse (approximately 15% of the original corpus).'
Section 5.4: 'Although the model is less accurate that a high-precision grammar-based parser on a test set of sentences parsable by that grammar, our model is an order of magnitude faster.'
No mention of out-of-domain evaluation or evaluation on ERG-unparseable sentences.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Evaluate on sentences that ERG cannot parse to demonstrate true coverage advantage. Evaluate on out-of-domain text (e.g., web text, speech) to assess generalization. Report coverage explicitly as percentage of sentences with valid parses.

concerns.title: Greedy decoding may miss better parses; no beam search comparison
concerns.description: The paper uses greedy decoding without exploring beam search or other search strategies. Greedy decoding may miss better parses reachable via non-greedy paths. No comparison to beam search is provided.
evidence: Section 4.3: 'We perform greedy decoding. For the stack-based model we ensure that if the stack is empty, the next transition predicted has to be shift. For the other models we ensure that the output is well-formed during post-processing by robustly skipping over out-of-place symbols or inserting missing ones.'
No mention of beam search or other search strategies.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Implement beam search and compare to greedy decoding. Report oracle accuracy with beam search to estimate potential improvement. Discuss trade-offs between speed and accuracy.

concerns.title: Oracle errors (1-2% EDM) and tokenization mismatches limit achievable accuracy
concerns.description: Oracle errors of 1-2% EDM represent an upper bound on parser performance. Tokenization mismatches between the system and ERG further limit achievable accuracy. These limitations are acknowledged but not quantified or addressed.
evidence: Section 5.4: 'For the arc-eager representation, the oracle EDM is 99% for the lexicalized representation and 98.06% for the delexicalized representation. The remaining errors are due to discrepancies between the tokenization used by our system and the ERG tokenization.'
No analysis of tokenization error impact or proposed solutions.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Quantify impact of tokenization mismatches on parser performance. Investigate whether using ERG tokenization would improve results. Discuss whether oracle errors are fundamental limitations or addressable issues.

concerns.title: Overstated 'first' claim with unclear definition of 'full-coverage'
concerns.description: The claim of being the 'first full-coverage neural MRS parser' depends on narrow definitions of 'full-coverage' and 'neural.' Prior work (Toutanova et al. 2005) achieved MRS parsing with grammar access. Definition of 'full-coverage' is ambiguous (all sentences in corpus? all phenomena in representation?). No explicit comparison to concurrent neural approaches.
evidence: Abstract: 'We propose a neural encoder-decoder transition-based parser which is the first full-coverage semantic graph parser for Minimal Recursion Semantics (MRS).'

Introduction: 'The only previous approach to parsing and disambiguating full MRS structures (as opposed to bilexical semantic graphs derived from, but simplifying MRS) were based on the ERG (Toutanova et al., 2005); this approach has high precision but incomplete coverage.'
Prior stage digest (reviewer_3): 'Claim of 'first' neural MRS parser depends on definitional boundaries; no explicit comparison to concurrent work.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify definition of 'full-coverage' (e.g., 'coverage of all sentences in DeepBank test set' or 'coverage of all MRS phenomena'). Acknowledge prior work on MRS parsing with grammar access. Search for concurrent neural MRS parsing work. Revise claim to be more precise (e.g., 'first neural MRS parser without grammar access' or 'first neural parser for full MRS structures').

concerns.title: Architectural innovations are incremental combinations of known techniques
concerns.description: The core architectural components (arc-eager transition systems, encoder-decoder models, pointer networks, stack-based features) are all known techniques. The novelty lies in their combination for semantic graph parsing, which is incremental rather than disruptive.
evidence: Section 3.2: Arc-eager transition systems adapted from Titov et al. (2009) and Gómez-Rodríguez & Nivre (2010).
Section 4.2: Pointer networks from Vinyals et al. (2015a).
Section 4.3: Stack-based features similar to Kiperwasser & Goldberg (2016) and Cross & Huang (2016a).
Prior stage digest (reviewer_3): 'Architectural innovations are incremental combinations of known techniques.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Frame contribution as 'novel application of transition-based parsing to semantic graphs' rather than 'novel architecture.' Emphasize the engineering contribution (batch processing) and empirical validation across representations.

concerns.title: Automatic alignment extraction for AMR introduces unquantified noise
concerns.description: For AMR, alignments are automatically obtained using JAMR aligner rather than being annotated. The paper acknowledges this introduces noise but does not quantify the impact or analyze alignment quality.
evidence: Section 5.1: 'We obtain alignments using the rule-based JAMR aligner (Flanigan et al., 2014).'
Section 5.5: 'The arc-eager model does not perform better than the top-down linearization, which we hypothesize is due to noise in the automatically-obtained alignments.'
No analysis of alignment quality or error rates.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Evaluate alignment quality (e.g., compare to manual alignments if available). Analyze impact of alignment errors on parser performance. Consider alternative alignment methods or error correction strategies.

concerns.title: Preprocessing dependencies (lemmatization, POS tagging, NER) not evaluated for robustness
concerns.description: The parser depends on Stanford CoreNLP for tokenization, lemmatization, POS tagging, and NER. No error analysis of preprocessing errors or evaluation of robustness to preprocessing mistakes.
evidence: Section 3.3: 'We use the Stanford CoreNLP toolkit (Manning et al., 2014) to tokenize and lemmatize sentences, and tag tokens with the Stanford Named Entity Recognizer (Finkel et al., 2005).'
No mention of preprocessing error rates or impact on parser performance.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Evaluate preprocessing error rates and their impact on parser performance. Consider using gold preprocessing (if available) to estimate upper bound. Discuss generalization to languages without reliable lemmatizers.

comparable_works.relevance: Foundational work on neural transition-based dependency parsing using BiLSTM features.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar: Uses BiLSTM encoder and stack-based features for transition-based parsing. Different: Applies to dependency parsing (trees) rather than semantic graphs; uses soft attention rather than hard attention.
comparable_works.source_trace: Retrieved from external literature corpus; cited in paper Section 4.3 and 5.3.

comparable_works.relevance: Prior work on arc-eager AMR parsing using neural methods.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar: Uses arc-eager transition system for semantic graph parsing. Different: Narrowly defined for AMR; no comparison to other semantic representations; no hard attention mechanism.
comparable_works.source_trace: Cited in paper Section 3.2 and 5.5; mentioned in prior stage digests.

comparable_works.relevance: Foundational work on pointer networks and neural constituency parsing.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar: Uses pointer networks for alignment prediction; encoder-decoder architecture. Different: Applies to constituency parsing rather than semantic graphs.
comparable_works.source_trace: Cited in paper Section 4.2 and 3.1.

comparable_works.relevance: Prior work on MRS parsing using grammar-based approach (ERG).
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar: Parses full MRS structures. Different: Grammar-based (requires ERG); incomplete coverage; no neural methods.
comparable_works.source_trace: Cited in paper Introduction as baseline for comparison.

comparable_works.relevance: Prior neural AMR parsers using sequence-to-sequence approaches.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar: Neural approaches to semantic graph parsing. Different: Sequence-to-sequence rather than transition-based; no hard attention or stack features.
comparable_works.source_trace: Cited in paper Section 5.5 as prior neural AMR parsers.

uncertainty_flags: Claim of 'first' neural MRS parser depends on narrow definitions; concurrent work may exist.
Hard attention superiority is shown on DMRS but contradicted on AMR; generalization unclear.
Stack-based improvement is modest (0.63 EDM) and statistical significance not tested.
Speedup comparison conflates GPU hardware with batching; unbatched speedup is only 5.6x.
MRS vs AMR parseability comparison conflates representation difficulty with training data quality (inter-annotator agreement 0.94 vs 0.71).
AMR results substantially weaker than MRS (60.11% vs 86.50% Smatch), suggesting architecture may be MRS-specific.
Automatic alignment extraction for AMR introduces noise; impact not quantified.
Oracle errors (1-2% EDM) and tokenization mismatches limit achievable accuracy.
Greedy decoding may miss better parses; no comparison to beam search.
Test set biased toward sentences parsable by ERG; 15% coverage gap means evaluation incomplete.
No human evaluation of parse quality; metrics may not capture all aspects of semantic correctness.
Pre-trained embedding contribution not ablated; impact unknown.
Generalization to out-of-domain text, unseen predicates, and rare phenomena not directly evaluated.
Comparison to state-of-the-art AMR parsers (CAMR) is unfair due to use of external resources (syntax, SRL).
Preprocessing dependencies (lemmatization, POS tagging, NER) not evaluated for robustness.
alternative_interpretations: The modest improvements over baselines (0.44-1.22 EDM) may not be statistically significant, suggesting the architectural innovations provide limited practical benefit.

The contradictory results between MRS and AMR (hard attention superior on DMRS but not AMR) suggest the architecture is optimized for MRS-like representations rather than being a general semantic graph parser.

The weak AMR results (60.11% Smatch) compared to MRS (86.50% Smatch) may reflect fundamental limitations of the architecture for non-compositional representations rather than representation difficulty.
The speedup claim (70x) is primarily due to GPU hardware and batching rather than algorithmic improvements; unbatched speedup (5.6x) is more modest.
The MRS vs AMR parseability claim may reflect differences in training data quality (inter-annotator agreement, grammar-derived annotations) rather than inherent representation difficulty.
The 'full-coverage' claim may be overstated; coverage is only demonstrated on sentences parsable by ERG, not on the full corpus or out-of-domain text.
The architectural innovations are incremental combinations of known techniques (arc-eager, encoder-decoder, pointer networks, stack features) rather than fundamentally novel contributions.
The paper's main contribution may be empirical validation that neural methods can parse MRS at scale, rather than novel architectural or algorithmic innovations.
transparency_notes: The paper acknowledges oracle errors (1-2% EDM) and tokenization mismatches but does not quantify their impact or propose solutions.
The paper acknowledges that automatic alignment extraction for AMR introduces noise but does not quantify the impact.
The paper acknowledges that arc-eager does not outperform top-down for AMR, contradicting the general claim.
The paper acknowledges that concept prediction is a weakness of the AMR model.
The paper acknowledges that the test set is biased toward sentences parsable by ERG (15% coverage gap).

The novelty lies in the application domain (semantic graphs) and the engineering contribution (batch processing) rather than in fundamental algorithmic or architectural innovations. The paper's main contribution is empirical validation that neural methods can parse MRS at scale without grammar access, which is valuable but not groundbreaking.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: This paper proposes a neural encoder-decoder transition-based parser for semantic graph parsing (MRS/DMRS/EDS/AMR), combining arc-eager transition systems with hard attention pointer networks and stack-based features. The core contribution is architecturally sound and well-motivated: arc-eager linearization adapted for joint node/alignment prediction, hard attention for supervised alignment prediction, and stack-based features for transition system state representation. Empirical results on MRS/DMRS/EDS are solid (85.48% EDM on DMRS test set), with comprehensive evaluation across multiple representations and systematic ablation studies. The practical engineering contribution (GPU batch processing enabling 70x speedup) is valuable. However, the paper overstates novelty and generalizability claims while undersupporting key assertions with rigorous evidence. Critical concerns include: (1) lack of statistical significance testing for modest improvements (0.44–1.22 EDM); (2) contradictory results between MRS and AMR (hard attention superior on DMRS but not AMR, arc-eager superior on DMRS but not AMR), suggesting representation-specific rather than general principles; (3) misleading speedup claim conflating GPU hardware with batching (unbatched speedup is only 5.6x); (4) problematic MRS vs AMR parseability claim conflating representation difficulty with training data quality (DeepBank inter-annotator agreement 0.94 vs AMR 0.71); (5) substantially weaker AMR results (60.11% Smatch vs 86.50% DMRS Smatch) suggesting architecture may be MRS-specific; (6) incomplete evaluation (15% coverage gap, no out-of-domain testing, no human evaluation, greedy decoding only). The paper makes solid incremental contributions to semantic parsing but requires substantial revisions to address methodological concerns and clarify overstated claims.
strengths: Novel architectural synthesis: Arc-eager transition systems combined with hard attention pointer networks and stack-based features represent a coherent and well-motivated design for semantic graph parsing. The adaptation of transition-based parsing to generate nodes incrementally (rather than assuming fixed nodes) is non-trivial.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Evaluation across three MRS-based representations (DMRS, EDS) and AMR with multiple metrics (EDM, EDM-Pred, EDM-Arg, Smatch, Concept F1) and systematic ablation studies on development sets provides valuable insights into design choices.

Practical engineering contribution: GPU batch processing implementation of stack-based transition-based parsing in static computation graphs enables significant speedup (70x batched, 5.6x unbatched) and practical deployment.

Clear presentation: Section 2 provides unified framework for semantic graphs; Section 3 clearly describes transition system and linearization strategies; Figures 1–3 effectively illustrate representations and transition sequences.

Honest acknowledgment of limitations: Paper transparently reports oracle errors (1–2% EDM), tokenization mismatches, end-span alignment weakness, and noise in automatic AMR alignments, contributing to credibility.

Solid technical foundation: Transition system is well-designed for semantic graphs with clear oracle definition, handling of non-planar dependencies via cross-arc transitions, and natural interpretation of alignment prediction.
limitations: Lack of statistical significance testing: Reported improvements are modest (0.44–1.22 EDM) and lack statistical significance tests. Hard attention vs soft attention on DMRS shows 1.22 EDM improvement (81.53% to 82.75%), stack-based improvement is 0.63 EDM (84.65% to 85.28%), unlexicalized vs lexicalized is 0.28–1.21 EDM. Without significance testing, confidence in these improvements is limited. This is a major methodological concern flagged by all reviewers.

Contradictory results between MRS and AMR undermine generalizability claims: Hard attention is claimed to outperform soft attention, but AMR results show soft attention performing comparably or better (59.88% vs 59.83% Smatch). Arc-eager is claimed to outperform top-down, but AMR results show top-down performing comparably or better (59.88% vs 59.83% Smatch). These contradictions suggest the architecture may be MRS-specific rather than general, contradicting claims about generality.

Misleading speedup comparison conflating multiple factors: The claim of 'order of magnitude speedup' (70x) conflates GPU hardware with batching. Unbatched speedup is only 5.6x (41.63 tokens/sec vs 7.47 tokens/sec). ACE speed varies with configuration (11.07–15.11 tokens/sec at different coverage levels), reducing speedup to 3.5–7x. Comparison uses slowest ACE configuration. Batch processing is not applicable to all scenarios (online/streaming). Hardware differences (GPU vs CPU) confound the comparison. This conflation is flagged by all reviewers as a significant issue.
open_questions: Why do hard attention and arc-eager linearization work well for DMRS but not for AMR? The paper acknowledges that arc-eager does not outperform top-down for AMR and hypothesizes this is due to noise in automatically-obtained alignments, but does not provide deeper investigation. Is the architecture fundamentally mismatched for non-compositional representations like AMR, or is the issue specific to alignment quality? This question is critical for assessing whether the approach is truly general or MRS-specific.

What is the precise definition of 'full-coverage' in the claim of 'first full-coverage neural MRS parser'? Does it mean coverage of all sentences in a corpus, all phenomena within a representation, or coverage on ERG-parseable sentences? The paper does not explicitly define this, and the claim depends on this definition. Additionally, the paper evaluates only on sentences parsable by ERG (85% of original corpus); what is the parser's performance on the 15% of sentences that ERG cannot parse?

How much of the 13–14 percentage point gap between oracle EDM (98.06%) and achieved EDM (85.48%) is due to oracle errors and tokenization mismatches versus other sources of error (alignment prediction, predicate prediction, structural errors)? The paper reports oracle errors but does not quantify their impact on final performance or discuss whether they represent fundamental limitations.

What is the quality of automatically-obtained alignments for AMR, and how much does alignment noise degrade parser performance? The paper acknowledges automatic alignments introduce noise but does not quantify alignment quality or error propagation. Evaluating on gold alignments (if available) would clarify whether alignment noise is a fundamental limitation or an addressable issue.

Does greedy decoding achieve near-optimal performance, or would beam search substantially improve results? The paper uses greedy decoding without exploring beam search or other search strategies. Comparison to beam search (beam size 4–8) would clarify whether greedy decoding is a significant limitation.

How does the parser generalize to out-of-domain text, unseen predicates, and rare phenomena? The paper claims unlexicalized predicates generalize better but does not directly evaluate on out-of-vocabulary predicates or rare phenomena. Direct evaluation on these subsets would validate generalization claims.

source_trace: Claim C1 ('First full-coverage neural MRS parser'): Abstract and Introduction (lines 1–150); prior work Toutanova et al. (2005) cited as baseline; no explicit comparison to concurrent neural approaches provided.

Claim C2 ('Hard attention outperforms soft attention'): Table 2 shows DMRS results (TD soft 81.53 vs TD hard 82.75 EDM); Table 5 shows AMR results (TD soft delex 59.88 vs AE hard delex 59.83 Smatch); Section 4.2 provides motivation for hard attention.

Claim C3 ('Stack-based features improve'): Table 2 shows AE hard 84.65 vs AE stack 85.28 EDM (development); abstract claims improvement from 79.68% to 84.16% but baseline not explicitly identified in tables.

Claim C4 ('Order of magnitude speedup'): Section 5.4 reports 529.42 tokens/sec (batched) vs 7.47 tokens/sec (ACE); unbatched version 41.63 tokens/sec; ACE speed varies with configuration (11.07–15.11 tokens/sec).

Claim C5 ('MRS more parseable than AMR'): Abstract and Introduction cite 86.69% Smatch (MRS) vs 83% upper bound (AMR); Section 5.1 reports inter-annotator agreement 0.94 (DeepBank) vs 0.71 (AMR); Table 3 shows DMRS 86.50% Smatch; Table 6 shows AMR 60.11% Smatch.
Claim C6 ('Arc-eager outperforms top-down'): Table 1 shows TD unlex 81.72 vs AE delex 82.56 EDM (development); Table 5 shows AE hard delex 59.83 vs TD soft delex 59.88 Smatch (AMR).
Claim C7 ('Unlexicalized predicates generalize better'): Table 1 shows TD lex 81.44 vs TD unlex 81.72 EDM; AE lex 81.35 vs AE delex 82.56 EDM; Section 5.4 provides motivation.
Claim C8 ('Monotone ordering better for DMRS'): Section 5.4 reports 0.44 EDM improvement for monotone vs in-order; development set only, no test set results.
Claim C9 ('Neural parser outperforms previous neural AMR parsers'): Section 5.5 provides qualitative comparison to Barzdins & Gosko 2016, Peng et al. 2017; Table 6 shows 60.11% Smatch.

Claim C10 ('Model achieves full coverage'): Section 5.1 notes 15% of corpus lacks ERG parses; Section 5.4 acknowledges model is less accurate than ACE but faster; no explicit coverage evaluation provided.
Oracle errors: Section 5.4 reports 99% EDM (lexicalized) and 98.06% EDM (delexicalized); tokenization mismatches identified as source of remaining errors.
Preprocessing dependencies: Section 3.3 and 5.3 mention Stanford CoreNLP for tokenization, lemmatization, POS tagging, NER; no error analysis provided.
Pre-trained embeddings: Section 5.3 mentions pre-trained order-sensitive embeddings (Ling et al. 2015) for first 100 dimensions; no ablation study provided.
Automatic AMR alignments: Section 3.3 mentions JAMR aligner for AMR; Section 5.5 acknowledges noise in automatic alignments; no quantification of alignment quality.

(7) Comparison to beam search (beam size 4–8) to validate greedy decoding choice. (8) Quantification of impact of automatic alignment extraction for AMR on parser performance. (9) Evaluation of preprocessing error rates and robustness to preprocessing errors. (10) Human evaluation on sample of 100–200 sentences to validate that automatic metrics capture semantic correctness. Paper's core contributions (architectural synthesis, batch processing implementation, comprehensive evaluation) are sound, but presentation and claims require substantial improvement. With revisions, paper would be suitable for publication at a top-tier venue.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: Strengths to emphasize: (1) Novel architectural synthesis of arc-eager transition systems with hard attention and stack-based features for semantic graph parsing, with clear motivation for each component. (2) Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple semantic representations (DMRS, EDS, AMR) with systematic ablations on development sets. (3) Practical engineering contribution (GPU batch processing) enabling significant speedup for practical deployment. (4) Honest acknowledgment of limitations (oracle errors, tokenization mismatches, end-span alignment weakness, automatic AMR alignment noise). Weaknesses to address: (1) Add statistical significance tests (bootstrap resampling or permutation tests) for all reported improvements; report 95% confidence intervals; clearly indicate which improvements are statistically significant at p<0.05. (2) Clarify definition of 'full-coverage' and revise 'first' claim to be more precise (e.g., 'first neural encoder-decoder transition-based parser for full MRS semantic graphs without grammar access'). (3) Substantially revise MRS vs AMR parseability claim: acknowledge that higher MRS scores reflect both representation differences and training data quality (inter-annotator agreement 0.94 vs 0.71); conduct controlled experiment comparing parser performance on representations with similar inter-annotator agreement, or reframe as 'MRS is easier to parse with current methods given available training data.' (4) Investigate why hard attention and arc-eager work well for DMRS but not AMR; provide evidence for hypotheses about automatic alignment noise, non-compositionality, or architectural mismatch; revise claims to be representation-specific (e.g., 'Hard attention outperforms soft attention for DMRS, where supervised alignments are available and reliable. For AMR, where alignments are automatically obtained and noisier, soft attention performs comparably.'). (5) Separate hardware effects from algorithmic improvements in speedup comparison; report unbatched speedup (5.6x) as primary metric; acknowledge batching requirement and applicability limitations (batch processing not applicable to online/streaming scenarios). (6) Evaluate on sentences unparseable by ERG (the 15% coverage gap) and out-of-domain text to validate coverage claims. (7) Compare to beam search (beam size 4–8) to validate greedy decoding choice; report oracle accuracy with beam search to estimate potential improvement. (8) Quantify impact of automatic alignment extraction for AMR on parser performance; evaluate alignment quality if gold alignments are available. (9) Evaluate preprocessing error rates and robustness to preprocessing errors; report accuracy with gold vs automatic preprocessing. (10) Provide human evaluation on sample of 100–200 sentences to validate that automatic metrics (EDM, Smatch) capture semantic correctness.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
This paper proposes a neural encoder-decoder transition-based parser for semantic graph parsing (MRS/DMRS/EDS/AMR), combining arc-eager transition systems with hard attention pointer networks and stack-based features for joint node/alignment prediction. The paper claims to be the 'first full-coverage neural MRS parser' and demonstrates solid empirical results on MRS/DMRS/EDS (85.48% EDM on DMRS test set) with practical speedup via GPU batch processing (70x over grammar-based parser). However, the paper overstates novelty and generalizability claims while undersupporting key assertions with rigorous evidence.

Strengths:
- Novel architectural synthesis: Arc-eager transition systems combined with hard attention pointer networks and stack-based features represent a coherent and well-motivated design for semantic graph parsing. The adaptation of transition-based parsing to generate nodes incrementally is non-trivial.
- Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Evaluation across three MRS-based representations (DMRS, EDS) and AMR with multiple metrics (EDM, EDM-Pred, EDM-Arg, Smatch, Concept F1) and systematic ablation studies on development sets provides valuable insights.
- Practical engineering contribution: GPU batch processing implementation enables significant speedup (70x batched, 5.6x unbatched) and practical deployment.
- Clear presentation: Unified framework for semantic graphs, clear descriptions of transition system and linearization strategies, effective figures.
- Honest acknowledgment of limitations: Oracle errors (1–2% EDM), tokenization mismatches, end-span alignment weakness, and noise in automatic AMR alignments are transparently reported.

Limitations:
- Lack of statistical significance testing: Reported improvements are modest (0.44–1.22 EDM) and lack statistical significance tests. Hard attention vs soft attention on DMRS shows 1.22 EDM improvement (81.53% to 82.75%), stack-based improvement is 0.63 EDM (84.65% to 85.28%), unlexicalized vs lexicalized is 0.28–1.21 EDM. Without significance testing, confidence in these improvements is limited. This is a major methodological concern flagged by all reviewers.
- Contradictory results between MRS and AMR undermine generalizability claims: Hard attention is claimed to outperform soft attention, but AMR results show soft attention performing comparably or better (59.88% vs 59.83% Smatch). Arc-eager is claimed to outperform top-down, but AMR results show top-down performing comparably or better. These contradictions suggest the architecture may be MRS-specific rather than general.
- Misleading speedup comparison conflating multiple factors: The claim of 'order of magnitude speedup' (70x) conflates GPU hardware with batching. Unbatched speedup is only 5.6x (41.63 tokens/sec vs 7.47 tokens/sec). ACE speed varies with configuration (11.07–15.11 tokens/sec at different coverage levels), reducing speedup to 3.5–7x. Batch processing is not applicable to all scenarios (online/streaming). Hardware differences (GPU vs CPU) confound the comparison.

Open Questions:
- Why do hard attention and arc-eager linearization work well for DMRS but not for AMR? The paper hypothesizes this is due to noise in automatically-obtained alignments, but does not provide deeper investigation. Is the architecture fundamentally mismatched for non-compositional representations, or is the issue specific to alignment quality?
- What is the precise definition of 'full-coverage' in the claim of 'first full-coverage neural MRS parser'? Does it mean coverage of all sentences in a corpus, all phenomena within a representation, or coverage on ERG-parseable sentences? The paper evaluates only on sentences parsable by ERG (85% of original corpus); what is the parser's performance on the 15% of sentences that ERG cannot parse?
- How much of the 13–14 percentage point gap between oracle EDM (98.06%) and achieved EDM (85.48%) is due to oracle errors and tokenization mismatches versus other sources of error? The paper reports oracle errors but does not quantify their impact.
- What is the quality of automatically-obtained alignments for AMR, and how much does alignment noise degrade parser performance? Evaluating on gold alignments (if available) would clarify whether alignment noise is a fundamental limitation.
- Does greedy decoding achieve near-optimal performance, or would beam search substantially improve results? Comparison to beam search (beam size 4–8) would clarify whether greedy decoding is a significant limitation.
- How does the parser generalize to out-of-domain text, unseen predicates, and rare phenomena? Direct evaluation on these subsets would validate generalization claims.

Transparency:
- Paper provides detailed descriptions of model architecture, training procedure, and hyperparameters, enabling reproducibility.
- Paper acknowledges oracle errors (1–2% EDM), tokenization mismatches, end-span alignment weakness, and noise in automatic AMR alignments.
- Paper does not provide statistical significance tests for any reported improvements; confidence in modest improvements is limited.
- Paper does not provide human evaluation of parse quality; validity of automatic metrics for capturing semantic correctness is unvalidated.
- Paper does not provide error analysis comparing DMRS and AMR parsing errors; reasons for substantially weaker AMR results are unclear.
- Paper does not provide ablation studies for some architectural choices (pre-trained embeddings, beam search); contribution of these choices is unknown.
- Paper does not provide analysis of generalization to unseen predicates, rare phenomena, or out-of-domain text; robustness claims are not directly supported.
- Paper does not provide analysis of preprocessing error propagation; impact of lemmatization, POS tagging, NER errors on parser performance is unknown.
- Paper does not provide code or data; reproducibility is limited to description of methods.
- Paper does not compare to concurrent neural MRS parsing work; novelty claim of 'first' is not fully validated.
- Paper does not provide fair comparison to state-of-the-art AMR parsers using same external resources; AMR results are not competitive with CAMR.
- Paper does not evaluate on sentences unparseable by ERG (15% of original corpus); coverage claim is incomplete.

Our key in- sight is to represent natural language via se- mantic graphs whose topology shares many commonalities with Freebase. Graph-based parsers (McDonald, 2006) treat pars- ing as a search-based structured prediction prob- lem in which the goal is learning a scoring func- tion over dependency trees such that the correct tree is scored above all other trees. Transition-based parsers (Nivre, 2004; Nivre, 2008) treat parsing as a sequence of actions that produce a parse tree, and a classiﬁer is trained to score the possible actions at each stage of the process and guide the parsing pro- cess. Perhaps the simplest graph-based parsers are arc-factored (ﬁrst order) models (McDonald, 2006), in which the scoring function for a tree decomposes over the individual arcs of the tree. More elaborate models look at larger (overlapping) parts, requiring more sophisticated inference and training algorithms (Martins et al., 2009; Koo and Collins, 2010). The basic transition-based parsers work in a greedy man- ner, performing a series of locally-optimal decisions, and boast very fast parsing speeds. More advanced transition-based parsers introduce some search into the process using a beam (Zhang and Clark, 2008) or dynamic programming (Huang and Sagae, 2010). Regardless of the details of the parsing frame- work being used, a crucial step in parser design is choosing the right feature function for the underly- ing statistical model. Indeed, methods which learn from question-answer pairs have been gaining momentum as a means of scaling semantic parsers to large, open-domain problems (Kwiatkowski et al., 2013; Berant et al., 2013; Berant and Liang, 2014; Yao and Van Durme, 2014). Figure 1 shows an example of a question, its annotated logical form, and answer (or denotation). In this paper, we build a semantic parser that does not require example annotations or question-answer pairs but instead learns from a large knowledge base (KB) and web-scale cor- pora. Speciﬁcally, we exploit Freebase, a large community-authored knowledge base that spans many sub-domains and stores real world facts in graphical format, and parsed sentences from a large corpus. We formulate semantic parsing as a graph matching problem. We convert the output of an open-domain combinatory categorial gram- mar (CCG) parser (Clark and Curran, 2007) into a graphical representation and subsequently map it onto Freebase. The parser’s graphs (also called un- grounded graphs) are mapped to all possible Free- base subgraphs (also called grounded graphs) by re- placing edges and nodes with relations and types in Freebase. Each grounded graph corresponds to a unique grounded logical query. During learning, our semantic parser is trained to identify which KB sub- graph best corresponds to the NL graph. Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

The basic transition-based parsers work in a greedy man- ner, performing a series of locally-optimal decisions, and boast very fast parsing speeds. More advanced transition-based parsers introduce some search into the process using a beam (Zhang and Clark, 2008) or dynamic programming (Huang and Sagae, 2010). Regardless of the details of the parsing frame- work being used, a crucial step in parser design is choosing the right feature function for the underly- ing statistical model. Indeed, methods which learn from question-answer pairs have been gaining momentum as a means of scaling semantic parsers to large, open-domain problems (Kwiatkowski et al., 2013; Berant et al., 2013; Berant and Liang, 2014; Yao and Van Durme, 2014). Figure 1 shows an example of a question, its annotated logical form, and answer (or denotation). In this paper, we build a semantic parser that does not require example annotations or question-answer pairs but instead learns from a large knowledge base (KB) and web-scale cor- pora. Speciﬁcally, we exploit Freebase, a large community-authored knowledge base that spans many sub-domains and stores real world facts in graphical format, and parsed sentences from a large corpus. We formulate semantic parsing as a graph matching problem. We convert the output of an open-domain combinatory categorial gram- mar (CCG) parser (Clark and Curran, 2007) into a graphical representation and subsequently map it onto Freebase. The parser’s graphs (also called un- grounded graphs) are mapped to all possible Free- base subgraphs (also called grounded graphs) by re- placing edges and nodes with relations and types in Freebase. Each grounded graph corresponds to a unique grounded logical query. During learning, our semantic parser is trained to identify which KB sub- graph best corresponds to the NL graph. Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: Large-scale Semantic Parsing without Question-Answer Pairs Siva Reddy, Mirella Lapata, Mark Steedman School of Informatics, University of Edinburgh 10 Crichton Street, Edinburgh EH8 9AB siva.reddy@ed.ac.uk, mlap@inf.ed.ac.uk, steedman@inf.ed.ac.uk Abstract In this paper we introduce a novel semantic parsing approach to query Freebase in natu- ral language without requiring manual anno- tations or question-answer pairs. Our key in- sight is to represent natural language via se- mantic graphs whose topology shares many commonalities with Freebase. Given this rep- resentation, we conceptualize semantic pars- ing as a graph matching problem. Our model converts sentences to semantic graphs using CCG and subsequently grounds them to Free- base guided by denotations as a form of weak supervision. Evaluation experiments on a sub- set of the F REE 917 and W EBQUESTIONS benchmark datasets show our semantic parser improves over the state of the art. 1 Introduction Querying a database to retrieve an answer, telling a robot to perform an action, or teaching a com- puter to play a game are tasks requiring communi- cation with machines in a language interpretable by them. Semantic parsing addresses the speciﬁc task of learning to map natural language (NL) to machine interpretable formal meaning representations. Indeed, methods which learn from question-answer pairs have been gaining momentum as a means of scaling semantic parsers to large, open-domain problems (Kwiatkowski et al., 2013; Berant et al., 2013; Berant and Liang, 2014; Yao and Van Durme, 2014). Figure 1 shows an example of a question, its annotated logical form, and answer (or denotation). In this paper, we build a semantic parser that does not require example annotations or question-answer pairs but instead learns from a large knowledge base (KB) and web-scale cor- pora. Speciﬁcally, we exploit Freebase, a large community-authored knowledge base that spans many sub-domains and stores real world facts in graphical format, and parsed sentences from a large corpus. We formulate semantic parsing as a graph matching problem. We convert the output of an open-domain combinatory categorial gram- mar (CCG) parser (Clark and Curran, 2007) into a graphical representation and subsequently map it onto Freebase. The parser’s graphs (also called un- grounded graphs) are mapped to all possible Free- base subgraphs (also called grounded graphs) by re- placing edges and nodes with relations and types in Freebase. Each grounded graph corresponds to a unique grounded logical query. During learning, our semantic parser is trained to identify which KB sub- graph best corresponds to the NL graph. top_documents.title: Document 3
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Fresh reviewers
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: As a fresh reviewer, you should form your own opinion of the paper. Note that you will not initially see the previous reviews or the authors’ revision notes (new in August 2023), but after you submit your review, you will gain access to the old reviews and the revision notes (click on the “Previous URL” link in the submission metadata). At this point, you should check the revision notes to see whether any weaknesses in your review were previously identified, and if so, edit your review to explain why the revisions were not fully adequate to address the weaknesses in question. You may also consider whether the previous reviews identified weaknesses that you hadn’t thought of, and if so, whether you agree that they represent serious concerns meriting inclusion in your review.

Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Graph-based parsers (McDonald, 2006) treat pars- ing as a search-based structured prediction prob- lem in which the goal is learning a scoring func- tion over dependency trees such that the correct tree is scored above all other trees. Transition-based parsers (Nivre, 2004; Nivre, 2008) treat parsing as a sequence of actions that produce a parse tree, and a classiﬁer is trained to score the possible actions at each stage of the process and guide the parsing pro- cess. Perhaps the simplest graph-based parsers are arc-factored (ﬁrst order) models (McDonald, 2006), in which the scoring function for a tree decomposes over the individual arcs of the tree. More elaborate models look at larger (overlapping) parts, requiring more sophisticated inference and training algorithms (Martins et al., 2009; Koo and Collins, 2010). The basic transition-based parsers work in a greedy man- ner, performing a series of locally-optimal decisions, and boast very fast parsing speeds. More advanced transition-based parsers introduce some search into the process using a beam (Zhang and Clark, 2008) or dynamic programming (Huang and Sagae, 2010). Regardless of the details of the parsing frame- work being used, a crucial step in parser design is choosing the right feature function for the underly- ing statistical model. For example, the feature rep- resentation in Chen and Manning (2014) is a con- catenation of 18 word vectors, 18 POS vectors and 12 dependency-label vectors.3 The above works tackle the effort in hand-crafting effective feature combinations. A different line of work attacks the feature-engineering problem by suggesting novel neural-network architectures for encoding the parser state, including intermediately- built subtrees, as vectors which are then fed to non- linear classiﬁers. Titov and Henderson encode the parser state using incremental sigmoid-belief net- works (2007). In the work of Dyer et al. (2015), the entire stack and buffer of a transition-based parser are encoded as a stack-LSTMs, where each stack el- ement is itself based on a compositional represen- tation of parse trees. Le and Zuidema (2014) en- code each tree node as two compositional represen- tations capturing the inside and outside structures around the node, and feed the representations into a reranker. A similar reranking approach, this time based on convolutional neural networks, is taken by Zhu et al. (2015). Finally, in Kiperwasser and Gold- berg (2016) we present an Easy-First parser based on a novel hierarchical-LSTM tree encoding.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: Large-scale Semantic Parsing without Question-Answer Pairs Siva Reddy, Mirella Lapata, Mark Steedman School of Informatics, University of Edinburgh 10 Crichton Street, Edinburgh EH8 9AB siva.reddy@ed.ac.uk, mlap@inf.ed.ac.uk, steedman@inf.ed.ac.uk Abstract In this paper we introduce a novel semantic parsing approach to query Freebase in natu- ral language without requiring manual anno- tations or question-answer pairs. Our key in- sight is to represent natural language via se- mantic graphs whose topology shares many commonalities with Freebase. Given this rep- resentation, we conceptualize semantic pars- ing as a graph matching problem. Our model converts sentences to semantic graphs using CCG and subsequently grounds them to Free- base guided by denotations as a form of weak supervision. Evaluation experiments on a sub- set of the F REE 917 and W EBQUESTIONS benchmark datasets show our semantic parser improves over the state of the art. 1 Introduction Querying a database to retrieve an answer, telling a robot to perform an action, or teaching a com- puter to play a game are tasks requiring communi- cation with machines in a language interpretable by them. Semantic parsing addresses the speciﬁc task of learning to map natural language (NL) to machine interpretable formal meaning representations. Tra- ditionally, sentences are converted into logical form grounded in the symbols of some ﬁxed ontology or relational database. Approaches for learning semantic parsers

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
